<reason>PRO (B) controlled the shape of the debate. Its first rebuttal reframed the clash effectively: CON's own program (permanent surveys, ready DART design, bookable lift, negotiated protocols) is deployed infrastructure, not a "research niche," so CON was really only contesting the standing impactor bus. B then narrowed the fight to the few-hundred-meter "dead zone" with years, not decades, of warning, and its pressure question forced CON into a concrete seven-year timeline. B's closing exploited that timeline sharply: every year spoken for, and the "crash funding when a city is named" premise fails because no city is named at year one. CON fought well — the scout-dependency point, the dubious "same bus is a gravity tractor" claim, the physics-can't-be-bound legal critique, and the opportunity-cost line were real hits — but CON never squarely answered why its position isn't already most of the motion, and its closing did not address B's "no city named early" attack even though it spoke last. B's two clipped turns are a small execution cost and its gravity-tractor claim was shaky, but B made the decisive comparison (start early enough to clear Earth vs. late partial push that chooses a country) clearer and easier to vote on.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B3.2/B5.1-B5.4: PRO's seven-year scenario forced CON to lay out a specific timeline (A4.2), and PRO's closing turned it against CON — a plan with zero slack that depends on crash funding triggered by certainty that only arrives late, manufacturing the very risk-corridor fight CON feared. CON's counter that the ready bus still waits on scout data (A5.2) blunted but did not neutralize this.</best_rebuttal>
